claims.text: The moderate hardness and strength combined with favorable ductility in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is governed by a simple solid-solution microstructure.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a single-phase FCC solid solution without significant precipitation or nanoscale ordering.
The target CoCrFeNiTi solid solution lacks nanoscale precipitates and internal phase boundaries that would effectively impede dislocation motion.
A single-phase solid solution without strengthening precipitates is weaker and softer than corresponding precipitation-hardened microstructures.
Secondary precipitates or ordered phases generally increase strength and hardness while reducing plasticity.
Controlled aging or thermomechanical treatment of CoCrFeNiTi can induce nanoscale precipitates or B2 ordering.
In the unaged solid solution, dislocations glide relatively freely because substantial short-range order and precipitates are absent.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered-domain boundaries act as dislocation-pinning barriers.
An aged, precipitation-strengthened CoCrFeNiTi specimen will have higher hardness and yield strength than the single-phase starting specimen.
The strengthening caused by aging will be accompanied by reduced uniform plastic strain or ductility.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable machinability.
The proposed mechanism applies from 25 °C to approximately 600 °C under both tensile and compressive loading.
Dislocation slip and possible twinning dominate CoCrFeNiTi deformation under quasi-static and moderate-rate loading within the stated temperature range.
The magnitude of strengthening and ductility loss depends on grain size, precipitate size and distribution, processing parameters, residual microsegregation, and minor second phases.
